questions.question: What resource does PgBouncer primarily protect by multiplexing client connections?
options: PostgreSQL backend processes and server connection slots
The application's HTTP worker count
The number of tables in one database
The size of every SQL result
questions.explanation: PgBouncer accepts many client sockets while bounding connections to PostgreSQL. Each PostgreSQL server connection owns a backend process and contributes to database concurrency.

questions.question: Two PgBouncer instances each serve three distinct (database, user) pools with pool_size = 20. How many base server connections can those pools request before reserves?
questions.explanation: The upper bound is 2 instances x 3 pools x 20 connections = 120. Capacity planning must include every independent pool and PgBouncer instance.

questions.question: When does transaction pooling return a server connection to the pool?
options: After every network packet
After COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends the transaction
Only when the PgBouncer process restarts
After the client application process exits
questions.explanation: Transaction pooling pins one backend for the transaction, then releases it at transaction end. A later transaction from the same client may receive another backend.

questions.question: Why is session-level SET search_path followed by a later transaction unsafe in transaction pooling?
options: PgBouncer does not forward SQL
PostgreSQL forbids search_path changes
The later transaction may use another backend, while the setting remains attached to the earlier backend session
COMMIT converts every SET into SET LOCAL
questions.explanation: Session state belongs to a PostgreSQL backend. Transaction pooling does not preserve backend identity across transactions, so use SET LOCAL inside the transaction or another reviewed mechanism.

questions.question: Which prepared-statement claim is correct for current PgBouncer transaction pooling?
options: SQL PREPARE is always rewritten across backends
Protocol-level named statements can be tracked when max_prepared_statements is non-zero, but SQL PREPARE and EXECUTE remain incompatible
Prepared statements work only when reserve_pool_size is zero
Every driver is compatible without integration testing
questions.explanation: PgBouncer tracks extended-protocol named statements, not ordinary SQL PREPARE/EXECUTE commands. Set the cache explicitly and test the deployed driver and PgBouncer versions.

questions.question: What does reserve_pool_timeout control?
options: How long PostgreSQL retains a completed transaction
How long a client waits before PgBouncer may open additional reserve server connections
How often PgBouncer rotates TLS certificates
How long DNS records remain authoritative
questions.explanation: Reserve connections become eligible only after a client has waited for reserve_pool_timeout. They are temporary overflow and still consume the database connection budget.

questions.question: Why must TLS and authentication be reviewed on both sides of PgBouncer?
options: PgBouncer terminates the client connection and opens a separate server connection to PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL automatically copies every client certificate into PgBouncer
server_tls_sslmode also configures browser HTTPS
Client TLS always validates the PostgreSQL server certificate
questions.explanation: Application-to-PgBouncer and PgBouncer-to-PostgreSQL are separate connections. Encryption, peer identity, credentials, and authorization need explicit policy at each boundary.

questions.question: SHOW POOLS reports growing cl_waiting and maxwait while PostgreSQL CPU and lock waits are already saturated. What is the safest first conclusion?
options: Increase every pool immediately
Disable query_wait_timeout
The database is the bottleneck, so a wider pool may amplify contention
Switch to statement pooling without testing
questions.explanation: Queue pressure plus database saturation means useful concurrency is exhausted. Diagnose query time and database contention before allowing more active backends.
